Name: Hardware Simulation / Synthesis Mismatch
Description:
The hardware design contains structures that are interpreted
		differently during synthesis than during simulation, which
		cause inconsistencies in security-relevant behavior between
		the synthesized implementation and the simulation.
ExtendedDescription: Hardware-description-language (HDL) code describes functionality which can be verified as correct using simulation tools. Synthesis tools then (automatically) convert this into a physically-realizable representation. Certain HDL code structures cannot be exactly represented, or have multiple valid representations from which the synthesis tool must choose. This can result in output which behaves differently to the (functionally-correct) HDL code. These "simulation/synthesis mismatches" may have security consequences.

WeaknessOrdinalities.Description:
This is a resultant weakness as the primary would be
			something like bad RTL coding practices or Synthesis
			optimization that then would result in a mismatch.

CommonConsequences.Note: The consequences depend on the affected hardware behavior. The synthesized implementation may make different control decisions, incorrectly update protected state, expose data, or fail to enforce restrictions that appeared to operate correctly during HDL simulation.

Entries.IntroText: A hardware designer implements an access control latch which takes in lock and unlock signals (which are only active for a single cycle) and a reset signal, and outputs an unlocked state signal. During operation, the unlocked signal is synchronously set high by the unlock input and set low by the lock input. The unlocked signal also intended to be low from startup and set low by reset.

Entries.BodyText: The following VHDL example is written for VHDL-93 or later.

The always block is intended to describe combinational logic for unlocked_next, which depends on four signals (lock, unlock, unlocked and reset). However, the sensitivity list is missing reset.


During pre-synthesis RTL simulation, this tells the simulator not to rerun the block when reset changes (only when the other signals change). The signal unlocked_next defaults to 1’b0 so the simulation sees the expected locked state and so the tests of the state after reset will pass.


Synthesis tools assume a complete sensitivity list and will therefore infer logic including the reset signal. When reset is high, the unlocked _next signal is (erroneously) set to 1’b1. This is a bug (as reset should force a non-unlocked state), which would be expected to be found in simulation. The design uses a two-process state machine style which masks this bug in the code during simulation, but allows it to propagate to the synthesized implementation.

The synthesized hardware exits reset in an insecure state (with unlocked set to 1’b1) and remains in that state until one of the lock/unlock signals changes state. An adversary can take advantage of this by exploiting whatever logic makes use of this signal to set itself to a secure state.

Entries.ExampleCode:
For combinational logic, ensure that simulation is triggered by every signal read by the block. This can be done by listing both inputs explicitly, but this is not recommended. 


 A safer and more maintainable approach is to use (in Verilog) always @*, which tells the simulator to include all signals used inside the block. In SystemVerilog, use always_comb. In VHDL use process(all).

Entries.IntroText: A hardware developer is debugging logic which requires the system to be in an unprotected mode. In order to enable their work, they have (temporarily) removed some code related to the "protected_mode_enabled" flag in a way that does not cause the simulations to fail.

Entries.BodyText:
The design assigns the security-relevant secure signal using logic that is hidden from synthesis by translate_off / translate_on or equivalent synthesis exclusion directives. Simulation tools treat these directives as comments and include the enclosed assignment, so simulation updates secure according to security_check(policy_ok, lock_ready) and appears to validate the intended protected-mode behavior.


Synthesis tools omit the code between the exclusion directives. The synthesized implementation therefore does not contain the same assignment that was exercised during simulation. This creates a simulation/synthesis mismatch in security-relevant behavior: the HDL model used for verification enables or disables protected mode using logic that is absent from the synthesized hardware.

Because the synthesized implementation does not include the same logic that was present during simulation, the hardware defaults to an insecure state. An attacker can take advantage of this to execute activities which would normally require some form of authorization, even though simulation results suggested that protected mode would be enforced.

Entries.ExampleCode:
Do not place security-relevant assignments inside synthesis-excluded regions. Any logic that affects protected-mode behavior should be represented consistently in both simulation and synthesis. 


 Limit synthesis translate_off / translate_on regions to simulation-only code that cannot assign, modify, override, or mask security-sensitive signals. 


 Carefully review all uses of translate_on/off directives. Ensure that developers can efficiently authorize their activities during development work, to avoid the temptation to bypass security features in this way.

Entries.IntroText: A hardware developer is designing a controller that manages whether protected configuration registers can be written. The controller includes states for reset handling, user-level operation, and privileged operation.

Entries.BodyText:
The design relies on a VHDL others choice or Verilog default branch to express recovery behavior for state values not explicitly listed in the state transition logic. In RTL simulation, the intended behavior is that unexpected controller states will transition to USER_ONLY, where protected configuration writes are blocked.


The error is assuming that this RTL-level recovery behavior will necessarily be preserved after synthesis. During synthesis, the state machine may be encoded, optimized, or transformed based on the states considered reachable during normal operation. As a result, logic associated with unused or faulty hardware encodings may be removed or altered, and the synthesized implementation may not preserve the same recovery behavior that appeared in RTL simulation.

If the synthesized implementation does not preserve the unexpected-state recovery behavior, the hardware may fail to return to USER_ONLY after a fault, reset anomaly, voltage glitch, clock disturbance, or other condition that places the state storage into an unintended encoding.


An attacker who can induce or influence such conditions may be able to leave protected configuration writes enabled, or cause them to become enabled, even though simulation suggested that unexpected state values would be forced into a state where those writes are blocked.

Entries.ExampleCode:
Do not rely on a VHDL others choice or Verilog default branch to guarantee post-synthesis recovery behavior for security-critical state machines. If recovery from unexpected state encodings affects access to protected configuration registers, the implementation should not depend on synthesis inferring and preserving that behavior from RTL alone. 


 For this type of security-critical controller, implement the state machine using a carefully-controlled structural or hand-synthesized representation where the relevant state elements, reset behavior, transition logic, and fail-closed recovery behavior are explicit. Be careful that the synthesiser does not infer a state machine from the crafted logic, and “undo” the work. Review the resulting gate-level or structural implementation to confirm that unintended encodings are handled as required.


 Perform post-synthesis simulations where faults are injected into the state registers and confirm the behavior.


 Perform formal analysis to prove that the behavior of these critical blocks has not been altered by the synthesis process.


 After the implementation is verified and validated, preserve it during integration so later synthesis or whole-design optimization does not re-encode, merge, remove, or otherwise transform the security-critical recovery logic.


 This approach is costly and design-specific, but it is appropriate when relying on ordinary RTL synthesis would create unacceptable security risk.

ObservedExamples.Description: The synthesized netlist incorrectly calculates memory addresses and fetches co-processor instructions, potentially causing unintended memory accesses or incorrect custom-instruction execution.
Debug-load requests should return complete load store unit (LSU) data, but the synthesized netlist returned incomplete data, potentially causing incorrect interpretation of memory state.
Instruction execution should update program-counter state correctly, but the synthesized netlist produced incomplete or undefined updates, potentially causing unintended control flow.
The program counter should update when the next-program-counter value changes, but the synthesized netlist allowed stale PC state, potentially causing incorrect instruction fetches or stalls.

ModesOfIntroduction.Note: This weakness can be introduced when HDL constructs, assignment ordering, synthesis directives, or tool-dependent semantics are used whose simulation behavior may not match synthesis interpretation. These constructs may behave correctly during HDL simulation but produce different security-relevant behavior in the synthesized implementation.

This weakness can be introduced or exposed during synthesis when the synthesis tool applies assumptions, optimizations, or transformations to HDL structures that cannot be physically implemented exactly as the simulation semantics dictate, or that permit multiple (valid) hardware implementations. The resulting netlist may behave differently from the model that was verified during simulation.

DetectionMethods.Description: HDL linting, rule-based static analysis, and HDL checker tools can examine source code for structures that may be interpreted differently by simulation and synthesis tools. They may identify synthesis-sensitive coding patterns associated with this weakness.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: This method can be useful for detecting potential coding issues, but it may not reveal whether these constructs result in observable behavioral divergence after synthesis. Moreover, a user may suppress or bypass these warnings and still produce the erroneous synthesized hardware implementation. This method can give false positives.

DetectionMethods.Description: Synthesis warning review can examine synthesis logs and reports for tool messages associated with possible simulation/synthesis mismatch. It may identify ignored constructs, unsupported HDL semantics, synthesis assumptions, or optimizations that could affect security-relevant behavior.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: Can reveal potential synthesis issues but relies on engineers interpreting warnings. Moreover, a user may suppress or bypass these warnings and still produce the erroneous synthesized hardware implementation.

DetectionMethods.Description: HDL-source-to-netlist formal equivalence checking can examine the simulated model and synthesized netlist for behavioral mismatch associated with this weakness. It may identify non-equivalent outputs, failed compare-points, state-mapping issues, or counterexamples under the checked constraints.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: Formal equivalence checking can be effective at the IP level for identifying mismatches between the source-code model and synthesized implementation. However, effectiveness may decrease as design complexity grows, particularly at the SoC level, due to state-space expansion and difficulty mapping non-equivalent points. Synthesis optimizations may merge, eliminate, or rename signals, which can also produce false positives or require additional setup to account for expected transformations.

DetectionMethods.Description: Cross-simulation across HDL-source and post-synthesis models can examine both abstraction levels for observable behavioral divergence associated with this weakness. It may identify mismatches when security-relevant behaviors are explicitly exercised.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: This method can be useful for detecting observable behavioral mismatches, but it may not exercise all execution scenarios and should be combined with other detection methods to improve coverage.

DetectionMethods.Description: Coverage-guided differential fuzzing can examine HDL source code and synthesized implementation models for behavioral divergence associated with this weakness. It may identify generated inputs or state conditions that expose synthesis-induced mismatches.
DetectionMethods.EffectivenessNotes: This method can be useful for detecting previously unknown synthesis-induced behavioral mismatches by exploring diverse execution paths through coverage-guided input generation. However, it may not exercise every reachable design state and should be combined with other detection methods to improve coverage.

PotentialMitigations.Description: Establish and enforce HDL coding and review practices that minimize differences between simulation semantics and synthesis interpretation. Avoid HDL constructs, synthesis directives, and tool-dependent behaviors known to cause simulation/synthesis mismatch, with particular attention to security-relevant logic.
PotentialMitigations.EffectivenessNotes: Avoidance of the patterns of code which can result in these errors removes the opportunity for error. However, in some cases (notably state machine encodings) this can be very difficult to achieve efficiently.

PotentialMitigations.Description: For security-critical logic, preserve intentional redundancy that is required for security. Examples may include redundant logic, triple modular redundancy (TMR) structures, Hamming-distance state encodings, or state-machine recovery logic. Use synthesis constraints, preservation attributes, carefully controlled structural implementation, or manual implementation of selected critical blocks to prevent this redundancy from being merged, re-encoded, or optimized away.
PotentialMitigations.EffectivenessNotes: This mitigation removes the structures which cause the problem, at the expense of additional design and verification effort, and additional risk of inclusion of other functional errors.
